old.name: Presqu'ile de Giens, double tombolo & Salins des Pesquiers
old.hook: A peninsula lashed to the coast by two parallel sand bars, one of only a handful of double tombolos on Earth (three to five worldwide), enclosing old salt pans; the sentier du littoral rounds the wild, wind-hammered west and south shores.
old.text: A peninsula lashed to the coast by two parallel sand bars, one of only a handful of double tombolos on Earth (three to five worldwide), enclosing old salt pans; the sentier du littoral rounds the wild, wind-hammered west and south shores. The salt works, run by the Compagnie des Salins du Midi, closed in 1995; the Conservatoire du littoral now owns the marsh (since 2001), a roost for pink flamingos year-round that peaks around 2,000 birds in late summer. The coast path you walk is the old sentier des douaniers, the early-19th-century customs path along which patrols once watched the shore for contraband, and it is the very right-of-way that a 1976 French law fixed nationwide as a public easement (a 3 m passage across private coastal land), later reinforced by the 1986 loi Littoral. Signal Salt production ceased 1995; marsh Conservatoire-owned since 2001, flamingos year-round; path is the old sentier des douaniers, and the 3 m coastal easement was set by a 1976 law (loi Littoral 1986).

old.name: Rade de Toulon (from Mont Faron)
old.hook: One of Europe's great natural roadsteads and the home port of the French Mediterranean fleet, seen whole from the summit of Mont Faron (584m): the harbour, the naval base, the Massif de la Sainte-Baume beyond on a clear day. A memorial to the August 1944 Allied landings in Provence sits at the top.

old.name: Sentier Blanc-Martel
old.hook: The Verdon's flagship hike: a roughly 16 km one-way descent into Europe's deepest river canyon, with steel ladders and a long unlit tunnel of around 670 m (bring a torch), from La Maline down to the Couloir Samson. A navette shuttle links the two trailheads so you don't double back.
old.text: The Verdon's flagship hike: a roughly 16 km one-way descent into Europe's deepest river canyon, with steel ladders and a long unlit tunnel of around 670 m (bring a torch), from La Maline down to the Couloir Samson. A navette shuttle links the two trailheads so you don't double back. Named for the two men behind the first full traverse of the canyon in August 1905: Paris speleologist Edouard-Alfred Martel, sent by the Ministry of Agriculture to survey drinking water for Provence (the Fontaine-l'Eveque spring), and Isidore Blanc, the naturalist schoolmaster of Rougon who guided him. The Touring Club de France engineered the trail proper, ladders at the Breche Imbert and all, between 1926 and 1928; Blanc, made a TCF delegate, worked it up until his accidental death in 1933, and the path was renamed Blanc-Martel in his honour in 2005. Honesty by negation: the path itself runs on the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence bank, not the Var; the Var owns the south rim (the Corniche Sublime belvederes above Aiguines). The wilder Imbut/Styx trail on the Var bank has been closed by municipal order since July 2022 for rockfall, so this is the canyon walk that is actually open. Signal First full canyon traverse by Martel and Blanc, August 1905; trail engineered by the Touring Club de France 1926-1928; renamed Blanc-Martel in 2005.

old.name: Chartreuse de la Verne
old.hook: A huge, near-black monastery built of green Maures serpentine, hidden on a forested ridge above the chestnut woods and reached only by a rough road; a working silent cloister with a partial visitor route.
old.text: A huge, near-black monastery built of green Maures serpentine, hidden on a forested ridge above the chestnut woods and reached only by a rough road; a working silent cloister with a partial visitor route. Founded around 1170 by the bishops of Toulon (Pierre Isnard) and Frejus (Fredol d'Anduze); the first Romanesque church was consecrated on 3 October 1174, pillaged by the lords of Bormes in 1416, and emptied when the Carthusians left for Italy at the Revolution (its property confiscated by decree of 2 November 1789). The green serpentine framing its portals was quarried nearby in the Maures and hauled up by mule, the local stone made monumental. Silent again since 1983, when the monastic Family of Bethlehem moved in. Honesty: much is enclosed, so you visit the edges of a living silence, not a museum. Signal Founded c.1170, church consecrated 1174, pillaged by the lords of Bormes 1416; monastic Family of Bethlehem in residence since 1983.

old_also.name: Chartreuse de la Verne
old_also.hook: A Carthusian monastery founded around 1170, isolated deep in the Massif des Maures and built largely from the local greenish serpentine stone. Listed as a historic monument since 1921; today home to the contemplative Sisters of Bethlehem.
old_also.text: A Carthusian monastery founded around 1170, isolated deep in the Massif des Maures and built largely from the local greenish serpentine stone. Listed as a historic monument since 1921; today home to the contemplative Sisters of Bethlehem. Signal Open most of the year, self-guided with a booklet: 11am-6pm June-August, 11am-5pm the rest of the season; closed in January and on religious holidays; adult €7. From about 21 June to 20 September the forest road (RD214) up to it can shut for fire risk - check with the Collobrières tourist office before driving. Silence is requested; dress modestly.

old.name: Plage Notre-Dame, Porquerolles
old.hook: 800 m of pale sand backed by Aleppo pines that run almost to the water, a 30-min walk or bike from the car-free village, and angled so it shelters from both the Mistral and the east wind.
old.text: 800 m of pale sand backed by Aleppo pines that run almost to the water, a 30-min walk or bike from the car-free village, and angled so it shelters from both the Mistral and the east wind. The whole island was a wedding gift. On 22 February 1912 Francois-Joseph Fournier, a Belgian boatman's son who made a gold fortune on the Veta Verde lode in Mexico, bought nearly all of the island's 1,254 hectares at auction for his wife Sylvia, then planted the eucalyptus, mimosa and umbrella pines that still shade the paths. European Best Destinations voted Notre-Dame the most beautiful beach in Europe in 2015, and it has paid for the fame: a 6,000-visitor daily summer cap (in place since 2021) and compulsory ferry booking now guard the freshwater table and the island's rich flora. Signal Island bought 22 Feb 1912 by Fournier; named Europe's most beautiful beach 2015; 6,000/day summer quota since 2021.

old_also.name: Porquerolles & Port-Cros (Îles d'Or)
old_also.label: 15–35 min by boat from Giens / Hyères port
old_also.hook: Two of the Golden Islands: Porquerolles for white-sand coves, vineyards and the Fondation Carmignac art foundation; Port-Cros for wild trails and no cars.
old_also.text: Two of the Golden Islands: Porquerolles for white-sand coves, vineyards and the Fondation Carmignac art foundation; Port-Cros for wild trails and no cars. Port-Cros became France's (and Europe's) first marine national park in 1963 — snorkel its underwater trail. Porquerolles was a 1912 wedding gift from industrialist François Fournier to his wife; the state bought most of it in 1971, and its Conservatoire vineyards preserve heritage vines.

old.name: Sentier sous-marin de la Palud, Port-Cros
old.hook: A 40-45 min walk from the harbour to the Plage de la Palud, then a free, marked snorkel loop (mask, fins, tuba) past six submerged interpretation buoys in a few metres of water, among grouper, wrasse and posidonia meadow.
old.text: A 40-45 min walk from the harbour to the Plage de la Palud, then a free, marked snorkel loop (mask, fins, tuba) past six submerged interpretation buoys in a few metres of water, among grouper, wrasse and posidonia meadow. Port-Cros became the first marine national park in Europe by decree of 14 December 1963, born of a donation rather than a purchase: the Henrys had run the island since 1921, and Marceline Henry gave a third of it (213 hectares of the western island) to the State on condition it be protected, with Andre Malraux carrying it through. The underwater trail here, laid in 1979, was the first in France. The real lesson: on this island you read the sea on foot, not just the land, and the fish are unafraid because nobody has speared them in over 60 years. Signal National park by decree of 14 Dec 1963 (first marine park in Europe); underwater trail opened 1979 (first in France).

old.name: Cap Taillat
old.hook: A wild sand isthmus tying a scrub islet to the mainland, reached on 2.5 km of coastal path through maquis, with a Neolithic dolmen (the Dolmen de Briande, excavated 1935, the southernmost in the Var) on the ridge above and swimmable coves on either flank of the tombolo.
old.text: A wild sand isthmus tying a scrub islet to the mainland, reached on 2.5 km of coastal path through maquis, with a Neolithic dolmen (the Dolmen de Briande, excavated 1935, the southernmost in the Var) on the ridge above and swimmable coves on either flank of the tombolo. It is wilderness today only because a Club Med was stopped here: a company bought 27 hectares in 1970 to build 400 bungalows and a marina, Ramatuelle's mayor called in the Conservatoire du littoral, and it bought Cap Taillat in 1987. A fire on 24 July 2017 burned some 550 hectares across Taillat and neighbouring Cap Lardier to ash; the cistus and heather maquis has been regrowing since, which is why the vegetation looks so young. Signal 27 ha bought for a 400-bungalow Club Med in 1970; saved by the Conservatoire du littoral (Cap Taillat acquired 1987); 24 July 2017 fire burned ~550 ha.
